Q: Why would one use WebAssembly in the Backend? A:

Please correct me if I'm wrong, but WebAssembly is needed on the frontend because browsers only interpret/compile HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, so using any other Language would require a special tool.

Correct.

But the backend doesn't have this restriction;

Incorrect.

If a library or tool has a WebAssembly it does not necessarily mean it can be consumed by the JavaScript runtime (Node.js, Deno, Bun, etc.). Not by default. See How can I use a C++ library from node.js? for an example how one would bridge C++ and Node.js.

The runtime can consume other tools, that is not a built-in capability. In order to use another language, the library/tool has to expose bindings for the runtime. These are usually supplied by the tool maintainer. You can do it yourself, if you are developing a backend JavaScript application. However, you might or might not have access to its code; you might or might not have enough information to provide the bindings for your runtime to use. While a WebAssembly distribution is readily available.

Another problem that compounds using tools written in another language: different runtimes will require different bindings. Even if a tool exposes an interface for Node.js, it will not be usable in Bun. And vice versa.

Since WebAssembly distributions will work across all runtime environments, it makes them more portable. Admittedly, this is probably a slim use-case but it is still an advantage over bridging over to native code.

The portability also means it is easier to ship and deploy the backend application. Depending on the deployment environment, supplying a native module might be hard or straight up impossible, if the system is locked down enough.

There is also an element of extra security. WebAssembly code runs in isolated and restricted mode. This can be important consideration - native code can be a vector of attack.

Overall, there is no one single reason to choose WebAssembly. There are plenty of cases you might choose to access native functionality through a bridge. Or you might not have this choice at all and WebAssembly might be your only option. Or you might have a choice and lean towards WebAssembly not because of one reason but combination of several factor.

Tech is, at the end of the day, a toolbox. Not everything requires a hammer - you pull the right tool for the job. Some times a hacksaw would be more appropriate, another time might call for hitting things with a screwdriver.

Q: Recommended key size and type for GnuPG? A:

I know the topic is old, but at this time, DSA 1024 is considered to be too weak, as is SHA-1. You should use RSA 2048 (for signing and encryption) and SHA256 (for digest). Normally, the symmetric algorithm used is AES256, which is good enough.

When encrypting, GPG gzips the data, creates an AES256 key and encrypts the data with it. It then encrypts the AES key with the recipient RSA or ElGamal public key and sends the encrypted AES key + the encrypted data in a pack.

RSA 2048 is said to protect data until 2015 or so, and RSA 4096 would protect data until 2020, based on the predicted computer power at that time. (I'm not totally sure about the dates, but it is logical that a 4096 bit key would be harder to crack than a 2048 bit one)

Q: Clang rejects constexpr construction through inherited CRTP constructors that GCC accepts A:

[basic.life]/2 says that

The lifetime of an object of type T begins when:

  • storage with the proper alignment and size for type T is obtained, and
  • its initialization (if any) is complete (including vacuous initialization) ([dcl.init]),

except that ...

And the initialization of the non-static data member is not performed before the base class's constructor returns, because [class.base.init]/13 says

In a non-delegating constructor, initialization proceeds in the following order:

  • First, and only for the constructor of the most derived class ([intro.object]), virtual base classes are initialized in the order they appear on a depth-first left-to-right traversal of the directed acyclic graph of base classes, where “left-to-right” is the order of appearance of the base classes in the derived class base-specifier-list.
  • Then, direct base classes are initialized in declaration order as they appear in the base-specifier-list (regardless of the order of the mem-initializers).
  • Then, non-static data members are initialized in the order they were declared in the class definition (again regardless of the order of the mem-initializers).
  • Finally, the compound-statement of the constructor body is executed.

So the lifetime of the data member value hasn't started yet when the write to it is executed in the constructor of Base.

[basic.life]/8 says that

Similarly, before the lifetime of an object has started but after the storage which the object will occupy has been allocated or after the lifetime of an object has ended and before the storage which the object occupied is reused or released, any glvalue that refers to the original object may be used but only in limited ways. For an object under construction or destruction, see [class.cdtor]. Otherwise, such a glvalue refers to allocated storage ([basic.stc.dynamic.allocation]), and using the properties of the glvalue that do not depend on its value is well-defined. The program has undefined behavior if

  • (8.1) the glvalue is used to access the object, or ...

Therefore the write to static_cast<D*>(this)->value has undefined behavior, which is not fine. Moreover, since it is evaluated at compile-time, and according to [expr.const.core]/2:

An expression E is a core constant expression unless the evaluation of E, following the rules of the abstract machine ([intro.execution]), would evaluate one of the following:

  • ...
  • (2.8) an operation that would have undefined or erroneous behavior as specified in [intro] through [cpp];
  • ...

the program is ill-formed since the compile-time evaluation involves a core language undefined behavior.

Clang is correct to diagnose this and reject the program.

Q: Is it safe enough to create a thread in a finalizer? A:

If your goal is to log an object's end-of-life, you can simply call some static method from the object's finalizer and if your goal is to detect the object's Dispose (or finalize) method NOT being called when the object is garbage-collected, I'd suggest using WeakReference to that object and then polling it to see if it was collected or not.

Q: How can I preserve tables, images, and nested lists when converting DOCX WORD to Markdown? A:

The problem is that document.paragraphs and document.tables are two separate lists. They do not represent the real order of the body. If you iterate them separately, tables will always be misplaced.

Iterate over the XML body children instead, and wrap each XML node back into a Paragraph or Table.

from docx import Document
from docx.oxml.text.paragraph import CT_P
from docx.oxml.table import CT_Tbl
from docx.text.paragraph import Paragraph
from docx.table import Table

def iter_block_items(parent):
    for child in parent.element.body.iterchildren():
        if isinstance(child, CT_P):
            yield Paragraph(child, parent)
        elif isinstance(child, CT_Tbl):
            yield Table(child, parent)

Then use it like this:

doc = Document("input.docx")

for block in iter_block_items(doc):
    if isinstance(block, Paragraph):
        output.append(convert_paragraph(block))
    elif isinstance(block, Table):
        output.append(convert_table(block))

That fixes the table-order issue. This is the important part: do not use document.paragraphs and document.tables separately.

For tables inside table cells, do the same thing recursively. Newer python-docx versions expose iter_inner_content() for block containers, which returns paragraphs and tables in document order, including inside cells. The docs describe it as generating each Paragraph or Table in document order.

For lists, don’t infer nesting from visible text. Word stores numbering/list information in paragraph XML, mainly under w:numPr. You need to read the paragraph’s numbering properties, especially the indentation level:

def get_list_level(paragraph):
    pPr = paragraph._p.pPr
    if pPr is None or pPr.numPr is None or pPr.numPr.ilvl is None:
        return None
    return int(pPr.numPr.ilvl.val)

Then indent Markdown based on that level:

level = get_list_level(paragraph)

if level is not None:
    indent = "   " * level
    text = paragraph.text
    return f"{indent}- {text}"

This is simplified; for ordered lists you also need to inspect the numbering definition in numbering.xml, because ilvl only tells you the nesting level, not whether it is 1. or -.

Images are not block-level elements in the same way tables are. They are usually inside paragraph runs. So preserve image position while converting the paragraph runs, not in a separate “extract all images” pass.

Q: NextFlow continuing processes when some inputs fail A:

There are plenty of very good options and exampled in the documentation on how to handle everything you ask about.

The simplest and proactive option is to ensure input files exist before starting, and is the top option in the channel factory docs:

workflow {
    // Intake input files
    input_files = channel.fromPath("pipeline_input.csv")
        .splitCsv(header:true)
        .map { row -> tuple(row.tag,file(row.input_filepath, checkIfExists = true)) } 
...

In some cases, I would prefer that the other jobs continue to completion regardless of whether or not other processes fail, since they are not inter-related.

This is possible as you can tailor the process error strategy or only pass intact files in many ways. IMO, these are good option if a file is corrupt or low quality and has to be ejected from the pipeline but you want the rest of the run to finish.

In this instance, it just sounds like you're missing files in your input csv. I would argue you should focus on ensuring your input data is intact before starting rather than trying to skip when files don't exist.
